analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers to disclose real prices and rebates, and extends community health center funding.
analysis.headline: A price transparency bill with 88 bipartisan cosponsors and a unanimous 49–0 committee vote never got a House floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The PATIENT Act would force hospitals to publish the actual prices they negotiate with insurers — not just sticker prices — and penalize hospitals that don't comply by at least $5 million a year. It would also make insurers disclose what they pay in-network doctors and what drug rebates they receive, require pharmacy benefit managers (the middlemen who negotiate drug prices) to show employers where rebate money goes, ban a PBM practice called spread pricing in Medicaid, and extend funding for community health centers and related health workforce programs. It passed the House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously but never came up for a vote by the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers who buy health coverage, and anyone trying to shop for care. Hospitals would have to publish negotiated rates, cash prices, and prices for at least 300 shoppable services in a free, machine-readable file, with penalties starting at $5 million per year for large hospitals that don't comply. Insurers would have to publish in-network rates and what they actually pay for drugs, net of rebates. Employers would see what rebates, fees, and discounts their PBMs collect from drug manufacturers — information currently hidden from them. Medicaid would ban PBM spread pricing, where the middleman charges the state more than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference. Community health centers, Teaching Health Centers, and the National Health Service Corps would get their funding extended [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying health bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires every hospital to publish, free and in a single machine-readable file, its gross charges, discounted cash prices, and the actual rates negotiated with each insurer for at least 300 shoppable services — the procedures patients can plan ahead and shop for [S3].

Gives the penalty real teeth: a large hospital that stays noncompliant for a full year would owe a civil fine of at least $5 million, and HHS would have to post a public list naming hospitals that were penalized, warned, or put on corrective action plans [S3].

Requires health insurers to publish their in-network rates for every provider, what they pay for drugs net of rebates, and what out-of-network items actually cost — updated quarterly, in files anyone can access without an account [S3].

Forces PBMs and insurers to report to employers (plan sponsors) every rebate, fee, discount, and consultant payment tied to their drug spending, with $10,000-a-day penalties for hiding information — ending the current system where the employer paying the bills can't see where its money goes [S3].

Bans spread pricing for PBMs in Medicaid — the practice of charging the state more for a drug than the PBM pays the pharmacy and pocketing the difference — and requires pass-through pricing instead [S2].

Requires hospitals, large physician practices, and practices owned by private equity firms or hospitals to report ownership, debt, and merger data annually, with fines up to $5 million per false or missing report, so regulators and the public can track health care consolidation [S3].

Requires Medicare Advantage plans to disclose payments to providers they own themselves, including incentive payments and health-risk-assessment data — the arrangement where a plan's owner also treats its patients [S3].

Extends funding for the Community Health Center program, the Teaching Health Center Graduate Medical Education program, and the National Health Service Corps, which staff clinics serving low-income and rural patients [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, health insurers, PBMs, and private equity/venture capital owners of medical practices would bear the costs. Hospitals would face detailed new publication duties, HHS audits of their posted prices, and civil fines of at least $5 million per year for large hospitals that stay out of compliance — the current maximum of about $5,500 per day would effectively be replaced by a much steeper floor [S3]. Insurers and PBMs would take on quarterly disclosure of rates and drug spending and annual reporting of rebates and fees, with penalties of $10,000 per day for failures and up to $100,000 per knowingly false item [S3]. Private-equity-owned and hospital-owned practices would face annual ownership and debt reporting with fines up to $5 million per report [S3]. The bill carries no new taxes; the cost is compliance and the loss of pricing secrecy.

drawbacks.text: Transparency alone doesn't cap prices. The bill requires disclosure but lets hospitals keep charging whatever they negotiate; whether prices actually fall depends on patients, employers, and regulators using the data, and the bill itself orders a GAO study of what more is needed rather than guaranteeing savings [S3].

The compliance burden is heavy and lands on providers of all sizes — hospitals, labs, insurers, and PBMs would all have to build and maintain detailed public price files and quarterly reports, and smaller hospitals and labs get only modestly lighter penalties ($300/day) rather than lighter duties [S3].

Much of the PBM and rebate reporting would not be fully public. Employers would see the data, but the bill lets insurers and PBMs place 'reasonable restrictions' on public disclosure of the reports, requiring them only to share them with federal and state agencies [S3].

The community health center and health workforce funding is a time-limited extension, not a permanent commitment, so clinics serving low-income patients would face the same funding cliff again when the extension runs out [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and broad: real negotiated prices for hospitals and insurance plans, and employer-level visibility into the drug rebate stream that today is essentially secret. The costs are compliance burdens on large health care companies and the possibility that savings depend on enforcement the bill only partially guarantees — HHS gets monitoring authority and a public shame list, and penalties rise sharply, but no provision directly lowers any price. On balance it is a well-designed transparency bill with unusually strong enforcement for the hospital title, weakened mainly by limiting public access to the PBM rebate reports. The bigger honest caveat is that it never became law, so none of this took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously in May 2023, but House leaders never scheduled it for a vote by the full House, and it died when the term ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers, chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on May 22, 2023 with Rep. Frank Pallone, the committee's top Democrat, as the two leaders of a bipartisan transparency effort [S1] [S3].
It drew 88 cosponsors split almost evenly between parties — 46 Republicans and 42 Democrats — within months of introduction [S4].
Two days after introduction, on May 24, 2023, the Energy and Commerce Committee marked the bill up and ordered it reported to the House, amended, by a vote of 49–0 — no member voted against it [S5].

The bill had been referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce. Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce never took it up, so the House could not consider it [S5].

After sitting for more than eighteen months, the bill's final action came on December 17, 2024, when it was referred to a Health subcommittee — a routine step with no schedule attached — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no House floor vote ever taken [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital systems, health insurers, PBMs, and private-equity owners of medical practices are better off because the bill died: none of the disclosure requirements, spread-pricing ban, ownership reporting, or multi-million-dollar penalties ever took effect, so their pricing and rebate arrangements stayed out of public view.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, insurers, and PBMs kept pricing secret

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan: 46 Republicans and 42 Democrats cosponsored the bill, and the committee reported it 49–0, with no recorded opposition at any stage.

industries.note: The bill targets the PBM business model directly: PBMs would have to disclose every rebate, fee, and discount they collect from drug manufacturers and what they pass on, spread pricing would be banned in Medicaid, and hiding information would cost $10,000 a day. Their revenue depends on the opacity the bill removes.

Hospitals would have to publish the real rates they negotiate with each insurer plus cash prices for 300 shoppable services, face HHS monitoring of their data's accuracy, and owe at least $5 million a year if they stay out of compliance — a steep escalation from the current ~$5,500-a-day maximum. Public disclosure of negotiated rates threatens the secret-pricing edge hospitals use in contract negotiations.

Insurers would take on quarterly publication of in-network rates and drug payment data and annual PBM reporting with daily penalties — significant compliance cost and loss of negotiating privacy. Some large insurers also own PBMs and provider groups, which the bill's ownership reporting would expose.

industries.industry: Private equity and venture capital in health care
industries.note: Firms that buy hospitals, physician practices, surgical centers, and freestanding ERs would have to report ownership, debt levels, and real estate deals annually, with fines up to $5 million per false or missing report — sunlight on the leveraged buyout model in medicine.

MA plans would have to report how much care and how many risk-adjusting diagnoses come from providers they own themselves, including incentive payments and at-home health risk assessments — the data Congress would need to police upcoding and self-dealing in the MA program.
Medicare lab providers would have to publish cash prices and their minimum and maximum negotiated rates for shoppable lab tests online each year, with $300-a-day penalties for noncompliance.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net clinics
industries.note: The bill would extend funding for the Community Health Center program, Teaching Health Center GME, and the National Health Service Corps — programs that staff clinics treating low-income and rural patients — though only for a limited period.
